prompt:
# Write one principle card

You are writing a **principle card**: one mechanism, stated so precisely that
somebody who has never seen your sources could implement it and somebody else
could prove it wrong.

The card is not the implementation. A later step turns it into a behaviour-tree
leaf, and that step will be given **your card and nothing else** — not this
prompt, not your reasoning, not whatever you were given below. So everything the
implementer needs has to survive inside the six fields.

## The system the principle has to fit

A Unitree Go2 quadruped navigating an indoor space it has no map of. Below the
behaviour tree sits an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy: the
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`, saturated
to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and `|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Nothing you write touches the
policy, the gait or the joints.

What the robot can sense, once per control step:

```
t                    sim seconds since the episode started
ranges               181 lidar beams over a full circle, metres, inf where no return
range_angles         beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
range_max            6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
pose_estimate        (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, never ground truth
pose_error_estimate  scalar metres — how wrong we believe that belief is
contact              bool — are we touching something right now
goal                 (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of those are traps. `pose_estimate` **drifts** on some scenarios — a seeded
random walk is added to it — and ground truth is never observable. `goal` may be
`None`, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still scored against it but
this robot has not found it yet; it latches once seen.

## The task family this principle has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is known, in an indoor space with no map. Walls and furniture occlude; the route is not a straight line and the obstruction is often not visible until the robot is close to it.

<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK BEGIN ---- -->
## What to base the principle on

The full text of a published paper is reproduced below. Read it and extract the
principle it establishes.

```
[PAPER TEXT REDACTED FROM THIS TRANSCRIPT — 35780 characters, sha256(pdf)=32a1b5f27a7fd3e9, extractor=pdftotext. The corpus is an input and is never committed (out/corpus/ is gitignored). The prompt_hash recorded beside this is the hash of the REAL prompt, so a machine holding the PDF re-renders it byte-identically and replay finds this transcript.]
```

Work from the document, not from your memory of it. Where the two disagree, the
document wins. Quote its own threshold, exponent or closed form where it states
one, and put the section, page or equation number in `span` so somebody else can
check it.

The paper was written about something other than a quadruped with a planar
lidar. Carrying it across is the `derivation` field's whole job: say what in the
original maps onto what here, and say plainly where the mapping is yours rather
than the paper's.
<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK END ---- -->

## What a card is

Six fields. `mechanism`, `trigger` and `derivation` are prose. `prediction` is
**structured**, because a prediction that cannot be decided automatically cannot
become a unit test — and this one will be run as one, with no human in the loop.

```yaml
id: <short_snake_case_identifier>
node_name: <TheLeafThisWouldProduce>       # CamelCase, verb-first

source:
  citation: <the reference this principle comes from, or the single line
             "(no source - the principle was devised, not extracted)" if it
             comes from none>
  span: <the section, page, figure or equation number where the mechanism is
         stated — the part that makes a threshold checkable. LEAVE EMPTY if you
         cannot point at a location you are sure of.>

mechanism: <what happens, and why it helps. The finding, not the implementation.>
trigger: <the condition under which it applies -> becomes the precondition port>
derivation: <how that becomes a rule for THIS robot and THESE sensors. Numbers
             belong here, with their units, and so does the reasoning that got
             you to them.>

prediction:
  statement: <the falsifiable claim, in words>
  metric: <what gets better>
  baseline: <goal_seeker or reactive_avoid>
  min_effect: <a number: the smallest effect that would count as support>
  cost_metric: <the metric this mechanism is expected to make WORSE>

confidence: <high | medium | low>
```

### `prediction.metric` — the closed list

The metric must be one the scorer actually computes, and one a **controller can
move**. These and no others:

| metric | better |
|---|---|
| `goal_reached` | higher (a rate over seeds) |
| `spl` | higher (path efficiency) |
| `min_clearance` | higher (closest approach to anything, metres) |
| `collisions`, `near_misses` | lower |
| `stuck_events`, `time_stuck`, `recovery_time` | lower |
| `time_to_goal`, `path_length` | lower |

`localisation_failures`, `optimal_distance`, `scenario` and `seed` are **not
available**: no controller can move them, so a prediction naming one is not
falsifiable about the node and the card is rejected at load.

`cost_metric` is the honest counterpart — the metric this mechanism is expected
to make worse. A mechanism that buys clearance with time should say so. It may
be empty only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs nothing, and you
should be suspicious of that belief.

### `confidence` — criteria about the SOURCE, not about how sure you feel

- **high** — the mechanism *and* its quantitative form are stated explicitly in
  a source you can point at; the span points at the equation, threshold or
  exponent itself.
- **medium** — the mechanism is stated explicitly somewhere, but the
  quantitative form is adapted: different units, a different body scale, a
  different sensor. The number is yours; the mechanism is not.
- **low** — the mechanism is qualitative and the derivation is entirely yours.
  Still usable, but it is your claim, and the card must not read otherwise.

## Rules

- **One mechanism.** A card describing two is two cards. This is not a style
  rule: the unit scenario that decides admissibility has to isolate one claimed
  effect, and it cannot isolate two.
- **No coupling to a specific scenario.** The leaf will run on worlds nobody has
  seen. The card may not name a room, a coordinate, a doorway or a map.
- **Do not invent a `span`.** An empty span is a result and costs nothing. A
  section number reconstructed from the shape of such papers is a fabrication,
  it will be checked against the document, and it is the single failure this
  pipeline exists to detect.
- **Do not invent numbers.** If a source states a threshold, an exponent or a
  closed form, give it and say where. If it does not, derive one, say the
  derivation is yours, and set `confidence: low`.

## What to return

One fenced ```yaml block containing exactly one card, and nothing else that
looks like YAML. Prose outside the fence — including, if it applies, an honest
statement of what you did not know.

response.text:
```yaml
id: brake_within_seen_free_space
node_name: LimitSpeedToStoppableSeenDistance

source:
  citation: >
    T. Fraichard and H. Asama, "Inevitable Collision States. A Step Towards Safer
    Robots?", Proc. IEEE/RSJ Int. Conf. on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS),
    Las Vegas, NV, Oct. 2003, pp. 388-393. HAL inria-00182082.
  span: >
    Def. 3 (Safe State) in Sec. V-A "Statement of the Problem", together with the
    braking-distance argument of Sec. I and Fig. 1 ("Collision states vs inevitable
    collision states"); the two corner strategies quoted are in Sec. V-D.

mechanism: >
  A state can be collision-free and still doomed: Sec. I, Fig. 1 argues that for a
  system that needs "a certain distance d to slow down and stop", every state within
  d of the wall is one from which "no matter what it does in the future, a collision
  will occur". These are inevitable collision states (ICS). Safety is therefore a
  property of state, not of position, and it is decided by comparing braking distance
  against free distance. The paper's second, sharper move (Def. 3, Sec. V-A) is what
  makes this usable without a map: at planning time an unexpected obstacle cannot be
  modelled, but it is known that it can only first appear on the boundary of the
  field of view. So the sensing-horizon part of that boundary (the paper's FoV_B, the
  dashed arc in Fig. 8-right, as opposed to the part explained by known obstacles) is
  itself treated as an obstacle, and a state is safe iff it is not an ICS with respect
  to the known obstacles AND not an ICS with respect to FoV_B. Consequence: a robot is
  only allowed to travel as fast as it can stop inside the region it has actually seen
  to be empty. Sec. V-D states the two ways to pass an occluding corner - "graze the
  corner while slowing down so that when you pass the corner, your speed is slow enough
  for you to stop before hitting a possible unexpected obstacle", or stay wide for a
  better view. This card is the first one: a speed cap, not a detour. It helps because
  the failure mode of an unmapped indoor run is exactly the paper's: the obstruction
  "is detected so late that avoiding it is impossible".

trigger: >
  Every control step in which the parent has produced a non-zero linear velocity
  command and a lidar scan for this step exists. The cap is computed always and binds
  (returns a strictly reduced command) only when the stoppable distance in the
  direction of travel is short; in open space it passes the parent's command through
  unchanged. It requires no map, no goal and no pose, so it is unaffected by
  pose_estimate drift and remains valid while goal is None.

derivation: >
  Mapping. The paper's car-like vehicle A becomes the Go2 whose only actuation is the
  Twist (vx, vy, wz); its "dynamics" are whatever the frozen locomotion policy does
  when the commanded velocity steps to zero. The paper's known obstacles become the
  finite lidar returns; the paper's FoV_B becomes two things in a 181-beam planar scan:
  (a) beams reading inf, whose unseen space begins at range_max = 6.0 m, and (b)
  occlusion shadows behind depth discontinuities, whose unseen space begins at the near
  side of the jump. Item (b) is my extension - the paper's FoV_B is only the sensing-
  range arc, because its vehicle's shadows were computed against a known map; with no
  map here, the shadow edge is the honest boundary of what has been seen to be free.
  Rule. Let (vx_c, vy_c) be the parent's commanded linear velocity, v_c = hypot(vx_c,
  vy_c), theta_c = atan2(vy_c, vx_c) in the robot frame. Build a point set P from the
  scan: for each beam i, r_i = ranges[i] if finite else range_max (6.0 m); additionally,
  for each adjacent pair with |r_{i+1} - r_i| > D_JUMP = 0.5 m, insert one virtual point
  at the bearing of the farther beam and the range of the nearer beam (the shadow
  mouth). Project each point of P into the travel frame: s = r*cos(a - theta_c),
  l = r*sin(a - theta_c). Keep points with s > 0 and |l| <= W = 0.25 m (Go2 body
  half-width ~0.16 m plus 0.09 m for yaw wobble and the frozen policy's lateral slop),
  and set d_free = min s over that corridor, or range_max if the corridor is empty.
  Required stopping room from the base origin is d_stop(v) = L_FRONT + v*TAU +
  v^2/(2*A_BRAKE), so invert it: v_cap = clip(-A_BRAKE*TAU + sqrt((A_BRAKE*TAU)^2 +
  2*A_BRAKE*max(0, d_free - L_FRONT)), 0.0, 0.8). If v_c > v_cap, scale both components
  by v_cap/v_c, preserving commanded direction; leave wz untouched. Numbers, all mine:
  L_FRONT = 0.35 m (base origin to the front of the body plus a 0.05 m skin), TAU = 0.20 m
  (two 10 Hz control steps of command-to-deceleration lag through the frozen policy),
  A_BRAKE = 1.0 m/s^2 (a deliberately pessimistic effective deceleration for a trotting
  quadruped commanded to zero; if the true value is larger the cap is merely conservative,
  which is the direction Property 4's "conservative approximation" of ICS also errs in).
  These give full 0.8 m/s only beyond d_free = 0.83 m, ~0.55 m/s at d_free = 0.55 m,
  and 0 m/s at d_free <= 0.35 m. Where the paper's ICS is exact, mine is a
  one-control-input approximation in the sense of its Property 4: I check only the
  braking control input, i.e. I ask whether stopping in a straight line is still
  possible. This is legitimate here for a reason the paper's forward-only point mass
  (Sec. IV-A, "North, North-East") did not have: the Go2 can hold a stand, so a
  zero-velocity non-contact state is never an ICS with respect to fixed obstacles, and
  "can I still stop" is therefore a sufficient safety test, not just a necessary one.
  Nothing here reads pose_estimate, so pose_error_estimate is irrelevant to it.

prediction:
  statement: >
    Wrapping the linear velocity command with this cap reduces the mean number of
    collisions per episode by at least 30% relative to the unwrapped baseline, over the
    same set of seeds and scenarios, because late-detected obstructions are met at a
    speed from which a stop still fits inside the seen-free corridor.
  metric: collisions
  baseline: goal_seeker
  min_effect: 0.30
  cost_metric: time_to_goal

confidence: medium
```

Two things I could not settle from the document, stated plainly:

- **The paper gives no number I could quote.** Its only quantitative content is symbolic (the distance `d` of Fig. 1, and the state/control equations of Sec. V-B, which are badly mangled in this OCR — variable names, subscripts and several equation bodies are rendered as glyph noise). So `A_BRAKE`, `TAU`, `L_FRONT`, `W` and `D_JUMP` are all mine, and the card says so. That is why `confidence` is `medium` and not `high`: the mechanism and the safe-state definition are explicit in the source, the arithmetic is not.
- **The frozen policy's actual deceleration is unobservable to me**, and it is the one number the cap's correctness hinges on. I chose 1.0 m/s² to fail safe (too slow rather than too late). If the real value were, say, 0.4 m/s², the cap would be optimistic and the prediction should fail — which is the right way for this card to be wrong.

One deliberate omission: the paper's Sec. V-D "stay away from the corner so as to have a better view" strategy is a *second* mechanism (a path-shaping one, and the one its RRT planner actually selected). It does not belong on this card and would need its own.
